prime.problem: Training has one goal: tokens per second per chip. Serving has three that pull against each other (throughput, time to first token, per-token latency), and optimising the wrong one wastes chips or loses users. Without a clear objective, every later trick is a solution looking for a problem.
prime.fits: Second card. It builds on perf-1's serving metrics and the prefill/generation split from the KV cache card, then names the three regimes and the three kinds of operation the rest of the chapter analyses one at a time.
expect: linear ops vs dot-product attention vs everything else
prime.goal: Pick the right objective for a workload, justify it with the reading-speed arithmetic, and say which kind of operation dominates a decode step at short and at long context.

attend: Which metric does each regime ignore, and what does ignoring it let you do with the batch?
How does the card turn human reading speed into a per-token latency budget, and which input to that is only a rule of thumb?
Why does a bigger batch help cost per token but not the experience of any single chat user?
In the per-layer FLOP split, which share stays fixed as context grows and which one grows, and why?
Why does the chapter analyse linear ops and attention separately instead of as one forward pass?

must: Throughput sets cost per token; TTFT is set by queueing plus prefill; per-token latency is one decode step → a bigger batch raises throughput but slows every user's step → the regime decides which constraint binds

Offline jobs are blind to per-sample latency → pack the batch until memory runs out; chat must beat reading speed (≈ 5.2 tokens/s ≈ 194 ms/token) with low TTFT → batch as far as that budget allows; edge serves one user → batch 1, fit the model, quantize

Linear ops' FLOPs and weight bytes don't depend on context, while attention's FLOPs and KV bytes grow with S → at batch 1 linear ops are 96.2% of a layer's FLOPs at S = 1,024 but only 76.3% at 8,192 → and KV bytes aren't shared across a batch → so the chapter treats linear ops and attention separately
elevated: The batch-1 ceiling is bandwidth ÷ weight bytes (209 tok/s for Llama-3.1-8B on H100) → it is about 40× reading speed → that headroom is what a chat service spends on batching other users
reference: the per-layer FLOP breakdown (Q 33.6, K+V 16.8, O 33.6, MLP 352.3 MFLOP)
the v5e and M3 batch-1 rows
Kiely's advice to run separate latency and throughput deployments

compress.prompt: Make a 3 × 3 grid from memory: rows are offline, chat and edge; columns are throughput, TTFT and per-token latency. Mark each cell matters or ignored, and write under it the one batching decision each regime implies. Then one line on why attention's share of a layer grows with context.
checklist: offline: only throughput matters → largest batch that fits
chat: all three, with per-token latency under ≈ 194 ms → batch within the latency budget
edge: lowest latency for one user → batch 1, fit the model
throughput and per-token latency trade off through the batch size
linear ops are fixed per token; attention FLOPs and KV bytes grow with context

retrieve.q: Explain why maximising MFU, the right target in training, can make a chat product worse.
answer: higher MFU at inference comes from bigger batches
a bigger batch makes each decode step longer, so every user waits longer per token
training has no per-sample latency, so it never pays this cost; the book says utilisation doesn't translate to better experience for individual users

retrieve.q: Walk through the reading-speed budget: from 238 words per minute to a per-token latency limit, and then to the headroom on an H100 at batch 1.
answer: 1000 ÷ 5.2 ≈ 194 ms per token keeps up with a reader
209 ÷ 5.2 ≈ 40× headroom, an upper bound because real engines don't reach the ceiling

retrieve.q: An agent calls the same model in a loop and feeds each answer straight into the next call. Which metric matters most, and does beating reading speed still mean fast enough?
answer: total response time (TTFT plus all decode steps) matters most, because a machine waits for the whole answer
reading speed is irrelevant: faster streaming keeps paying off when a machine consumes the tokens
so the batch must be smaller than a chat service would choose, at a higher cost per token

compare.q: perf-1 defines TTFT, TPOT and throughput; this card adds regimes. What does knowing the regime change about how you use the same three numbers?
answer: the metrics are the same; the regime decides which one is the objective and which are constraints
offline: minimise cost, no latency constraint; chat: minimise cost subject to TTFT and TPOT limits; edge: minimise latency
the same server config can be right for one regime and wrong for another

compare.q: This card sketches the latency–throughput curve qualitatively; the step-time card computes it. What causes the curve to flatten, and at which batch does it hit its end on one H100 at 2k context?
answer: early: the fixed weight read is shared, so throughput rises steeply
later: every extra sequence adds its own KV read, so throughput flattens toward bandwidth ÷ KV bytes per sequence
at 2k it ends when HBM is full: 238 sequences, 9,973 tokens/s, 41.9 tokens/s per user

predict.q: Push the per-layer FLOP split to a 32,768-token context at batch 1 (Llama-3.1-8B). Commit: is attention now under or over half of a layer's FLOPs?
predict.answer: Over half. Attention matmuls are 4 × 32 × 128 × 32,768 = 536.9 MFLOP plus about 5.2 MFLOP of softmax, 542.1 MFLOP against a fixed 436.2 MFLOP of linear ops: about 55%. Linear ops don't change with context; attention grows linearly with it. And the bytes tell the same story harder: that layer reads 134 MB of KV against 436 MB of weights, a share that grows with every sequence in the batch.

apply.task: Classify three workloads into a regime and pick a batching policy for each, with one number to justify it: (a) scoring 50,000 benchmark prompts overnight with Llama-3.1-8B on one H100; (b) a support chatbot on the same GPU; (c) a 4-bit model on a 24 GB laptop for one person. Then recompute the per-layer attention share at S = 32,768 to see how long context shifts the balance.
apply.done: Each workload has a regime, a batch policy and a justifying number (for example 63.9 GB free ≈ 59 sequences at 8k for (a); ≈ 194 ms/token budget for (b); batch 1 and ≈ 15 tok/s measured on the M3 for (c)), and your attention share at 32k is about 55%.
apply.hint: Attention at 32k per layer: 4·N·H·S = 4 × 32 × 128 × 32,768 = 536.9 MFLOP, plus ≈ 5 FLOP × N × S ≈ 5.2 MFLOP of softmax. Divide by that plus 436.2 + 0.13.
